output.title: Why data cleaning is not the whole job
output.body:
Data cleaning helps, but it is only the input side of a workflow. If your team fixes fields and still has to make the same downstream decisions by hand, the real bottleneck has not moved.

The useful question is not “is the data clean?” It is: what still needs human judgment after the data is clean? In a small business workflow, that often means categorising a row, routing it, approving it, or handling exceptions. Funny how software can sort the tidy bits and still leave the awkward ones on your desk.

So map one repeating workflow as input → decision → output. Then mark each step as rules-based or judgment-based. If you want a practical next step, do that on paper first: list the step, note where approval or sign-off is still needed, and record which parts are repeatable. If you find a long tail of manual decisions after cleaning, that boundary is often where automation fits.

Bareni’s own demo work includes controls like rule checks, exception handling, and human-only approval. That is policy and positioning, not a claim about customer deployments.

Start with the decision layer, not another cleanup tool.
